57	### D. The wrapping operators, `rung-wrap-operators`
58	
59	**The answers this rung follows.** Q2 = (a). (Section 5 of the batch record gives the question and both options; where this section says "under Q2 = (b)", that text applies only if the coordinator has written that letter here. How `NN32` and `NN64` bind the new operators is decided, not asked: section 5, U.)
60	
61	**The problem.** Under `walk`, `+`, `-`, unary `-` and multiplication on the fixed-width integers keep the low 32 or 64 bits of a result that does not fit, where the specification says "For integer results, overflow throws an `IntegerOverflow`" (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, `:195-196`). The specification gives code that means to wrap operators of its own, which "do not overflow": wraparound addition and subtraction `DOTPLUS` and `DOTMINUS` (`:205-209`), wraparound multiplication `DOTTIMES` (`:172-176`), a unary `DOTMINUS` beside unary `-` (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:376-384`), and on the unbounded `ZZ` the same operators as `+`, `-` and multiplication, since operations on it "never need to wrap or saturate" (`:369-370`); the parser reads the ASCII names as the specification's characters (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Literal.rats:263`, `:270-271`). The interpreter's library declares none of the three, so a use ends a `walk` run with "Operator ? is not defined" (ledger row 348). Code of the 2012 tree that means to wrap therefore spells it `+`, `-` or multiplication and relies on `walk` wrapping: four library files and six of the team's tests (row 403; `explorations/reviews/wrap-dependent-code.md` sections 3, 9 and 11). While it does, row 379's fix cannot land: with the ten signed natives checked, 11 interpreter tests stop with an uncaught `IntegerOverflow` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-overflow/REPORT.md` section 1). The compiled path throws on these operations already, so the same bodies throw there at the switch-over whatever `walk` does (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-overflow/JUDGE.md` section 3, point 1).
62	
63	**The decisions.** Pavol, 2026-09-26 (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:108`), the note's option 1, the specification's own way: the wrapping operators declared on `Integral[\I\]` and on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ` in the interpreter's library, "bound to wrapping natives of their own beside the checked ones"; the library bodies that mean to wrap and the team tests that assert or rely on wrapping "rewritten with them, every expression fully parenthesised since the operators' precedence is stated only among themselves, and the strided distance that must not overflow is reordered and keeps the checked operators"; the saturating family left for a step of its own. The fifth batch-5 answer (`:149`): the rung "also rewrites the intended wraps in Steele's `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss` (`:195-211`, unary `-` as 2^w minus a value, and the wrapping products) and any unsigned wraps in the library", "keeping the values and changing no output". Checking the natives, signed and unsigned, is rung O in batch 6, not this rung (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md:35`; `POSITIONS.md:149`).
64	
65	**What it declares.** In the layout `+` has in each trait, with the specification's spellings and not the compiler prelude's reversed ones (row 348; `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-overflow/JUDGE.md` section 5, step 1):
66	- on `trait Integral[\I\]`, abstract: `opr DOTPLUS(self, b:I):I`, `opr DOTMINUS(self, b:I):I`, `opr DOTMINUS(self):I` and `opr DOTTIMES(self, b:I):I` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:414-436`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:615-644`), which the range library needs, being generic in `I extends Integral[\I\]` (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1013`, `:1183`);
67	- on `ZZ32` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:646-702`, api `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:465-497`) and `ZZ64` (`.fss:704-772`, api `.fsi:499-535`): bodies bound to new wrapping native classes, four per width (add, subtract, multiply, negate) with today's bodies (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:98-120`, `Long.java:112-134`), written after the last class of each file so that no Java line an interpreter stack trace prints moves. They are new classes because batch 6's rung O changes today's classes in place (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-overflow/natives.patch`); `+`, `-` and multiplication stay on today's classes, unchanged;
68	- on `NN64` (`.fss:774-824`, api `.fsi:438-462`) and on `NN32` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:387-448`, api `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:82-107`): bodies bound to new wrapping native classes, four per width, with today's bodies (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/NN32.java:103-126`, `UnsignedLong.java:104-125`), written after the last class of each file, beside `NN32$Add`, `UnsignedLong$Add` and their siblings, which `+`, `-`, unary `-` and multiplication keep and which batch 6's rung O then checks in place (`POSITIONS.md:149`); the shape of the signed widths, and the one the team's 2011 compiler library gives every integer type (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:766-775`);
69	- on `ZZ` (`.fss:826-898`): bodies bound to the exact natives `+`, `-` and multiplication use (`BigNum$Add`, `BigNum$Sub`, `BigNum$Mul`, `BigNum$Negate`), since on `ZZ` the operators are the plain ones (`basic-integers.tex:369-370`).
70	
71	**What it rewrites.** Every respelled expression gives the value it gives today, because the wrapping operator is the arithmetic the site gets today, and every one is fully parenthesised: `DOTPLUS` and `DOTMINUS` have a precedence stated only against each other and against `DOTTIMES` (`Specification/appendices/operators.tex:215-224`), and "If no precedence relationship is stated explicitly" between two operators, "then there is no precedence relationship between those two operators" (`:27-29`). The sites are those of `explorations/reviews/wrap-dependent-code.md` section 9, cases (a) to (i):
72	- `Library/RangeInternals.fss`, the six range splits (`:1030-1031`, `:1045-1046`, `:1200-1201`, `:1220-1221`, `:1241-1242`, `:1265-1266`): `split-1` becomes `(split DOTMINUS 1)`, and `(lo BITXOR hi)+1` becomes `((lo BITXOR hi) DOTPLUS 1)`. The strided distance `... - lo - 1` at `:1201`, `:1221`, `:1242` and `:1266`, which must not overflow rather than wrap, is reordered so that 1 is subtracted from the split point first and `lo` after, and keeps the checked operators.
73	- `Library/Random.fss:235` and `:241`: `((mult DOTTIMES widen(state)) DOTPLUS add) MOD modulus`, and the same with `widen(newseed BITXOR p)`.
74	- `Library/ChunkedSparseArray.fss:76`: `popCount((mask DOTMINUS 1) BITAND fe)`.
75	- `Library/IntMap.fss:675-676`: `partitionL(((mn DOTMINUS 1) BITXOR mx) DOTPLUS 1)` and `(DOTMINUS p) BITAND mx`.
76	- `ProjectFortress/tests/HeapTest.fss:98`: `((c1 DOTTIMES n) DOTPLUS c2, n)`.
77	- `ProjectFortress/tests/intPrim.fss:21-22` and `longPrim.fss:21-22`: `(a.minimum DOTMINUS 1)` and `(a.maximum DOTPLUS 1)`. The assertions that `-` and `+` throw there belong to rung O in batch 6, since this rung leaves the natives wrapping. `longPrim`'s `a: ZZ64 = 0` holds a `ZZ32` (row 146) and stays as it is.
78	- `ProjectFortress/tests/QuickCheckTest.fss:89-90` and `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest.fss:16-17`: the associativity property stated of `DOTPLUS`, `((p DOTPLUS q) DOTPLUS r) = (p DOTPLUS (q DOTPLUS r))`, which still should pass.
79	- `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss`: every intended unsigned wrap, unary `-` as 2^w minus a value and the wrapping products and differences, at `:195-211` by the decision and wherever else the logging pass below finds one (by reading also `:155-157` and `:173-180`, and their twins in the file's `NN32` half, `:50-52`, `:68-75` and from `:89`), respelled with `DOTMINUS`, `DOTPLUS` and `DOTTIMES`.
80	- Any wrap over `NN32` or `NN64` in a library body that the logging pass finds.
81	- Nothing else. Code that must avoid overflow is reordered, not respelled with a wrap it does not mean (`wrap-dependent-code.md` section 9, "In general").
82	
83	**The test, first.** One new file in `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's corpus, in the form of `tests/roundBug.fss` (a component exporting `Executable` whose `run()` asserts), as rungs I and C did: `DOTPLUS`, binary and unary `DOTMINUS` and `DOTTIMES` wrap at the minimum and the maximum of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, and on `ZZ` equal `+`, `-` and multiplication; `ZZ64` values are made with `widen`, not from numerals (row 146); each assertion's message cites `opr-overview.tex:172-176` or `:205-209`. Captured failing before the edit (row 348's "Operator ? is not defined", exit 255). It is not an `XXX` file, and a file in that directory needs no `.test` file (FACTS.md, "An `XXX*.fss` in the interpreter corpus IS a gated expected-failure test").
84	
85	**No output changes: the comparison.** The rung's stop is any changed interpreter output, and before it reports, the rung shows there is none:
86	1. Every file of `ProjectFortress/tests/` except the new test runs under `walk` in three passes, base A, the edit, base B, one JVM per test with private caches, with rung O's runner and comparison (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-overflow/count-run.sh`, `count-compare.py`; its `REPORT.md` section 2). A file whose two base passes differ varies on its own and is judged by hand, as rung O judged its seventeen.
87	2. Under Q2 = (a), three things are normalised before comparing, and nothing else: the Java line numbers in a printed stack frame and an object's identity hash (`@` followed by hex digits), as `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-interp-coercion/compare-runs.py` normalises them, which is how Pavol read rung C's three changed outputs (`POSITIONS.md:106`); and every Fortress source position in a file this rung edits, mapped back to its base line through the edit's line map, because the new declarations move every line below them in `FortressLibrary.fss` and `FortressBuiltin.fss` (precedent: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/remap-lines.py`). Every normalised difference is listed in `REPORT.md` with its file, and the same list is a capture under `probes/`, so that it survives a refused report file (section 8). Under Q2 = (b), nothing is normalised.
88	3. Any other difference in a stable file, or any changed exit code, is the stop.
89	4. The logging pass, which reads no output: rung O's `probes/overflow-probe.patch` (each native prints a line where it meets an overflow, and still wraps), extended to the add, subtract, multiply and negate natives of `NN32.java` and `UnsignedLong.java`, is run as a classpath shadow over every file of `ProjectFortress/tests/`, over `ProjectFortress/demos/*.fss` and over the two microGPT check programs (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss`, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplCheck.fss`), on the base and after the edit, each demo with a timeout of 120 s and the ones that reach it listed. On the base it names every site that relies on a wrap: rung O's eleven files, and whatever batch 4's landed rungs added, since rung K's widened shift makes a `ZZ32` sum wrap at 32 bits where it used to be a `ZZ64` sum (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-4/RECORD.md`, "For rung O when it runs again"). After the edit the ten signed natives and the eight unsigned ones must meet none, which predicts batch 6's rung O count at zero on all eighteen; the pass's site list before and after is a capture under `probes/`, as rung O's `probes/overflow-probe-summary.txt` is.
90	5. Each changed file's outputs go under `probes/count/`, as rung O's do, and every pass is headed by the machine line (`explorations/protocol.md` section 6).
91	
92	**Files it may touch.** `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss` (the declarations above, nothing else); `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi` and `.fss` (`NN32`'s block only); `Library/RangeInternals.fss`, `Library/Random.fss`, `Library/ChunkedSparseArray.fss` and `Library/IntMap.fss` (the sites above, and any wrap the logging pass finds); `interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java`, `Long.java`, `NN32.java` and `UnsignedLong.java` (the new classes only); the six test files named above and the new one; its own directory.
93	
94	**Java or Scala.** Java and the library. `ant compileAll` before the test can pass, and `default_repository/caches/global.map` restored after it (FACTS.md, "`ant compileAll` deletes a tracked file"); the interpreter's caches wiped before every run that reads the edited library.
95	
96	**The checker count.** Predicted 125, unchanged. The stage reads `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `FortressBuiltin.fsi`, and both apis stop at their hierarchy errors (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java:268-272`; in the FortressBuiltin api `NN32`'s own header `FortressBuiltin.fsi:82` is among them, in the batch 4 gate's full checker output, which is not committed) before any check that reads a method's declaration, as rung K measured for its api lines (FACTS.md, "The interpreter's integer rules"). The rung captures the stage's table before and after its edit and declares the total it measured.

A difference the rung traces to its own respelling is the rung's to fix; one that the correct respelling leaves is the stop, and it is Pavol's to read ("changing no output", `POSITIONS.md:149`), not a judge's: the rung reports stopped with the list, as rung O did with its count. Row 348's interpreter half, since `walk` has the specification's wrapping spellings; its compiled half, the prelude's reversed spellings in 10 compiled test files, closes at the switch-over. 108	### S. The specification, `rung-spec-route-a`
109	
110	**The answers this rung follows.** Q5 = (b). (Section 5 of the batch record; under Q5 = (a), route C also gets an entry in the internal appendix's "Proposed Features" section, `Specification/appendices/future.tex:12`.)
111	
112	**The problem.** The specification (`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft, the project's standard) never states the rule route A keeps, that no type is a subtype of two different instantiations of one generic, and says the opposite (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-340`, `:365-367`); and its examples use shapes the rule refuses: three where-clause examples, `Nothing`, the root's algebra, three passages of the internal appendix, and the number tower (FACTS.md, "The specification's own examples that the multiple instantiation exclusion refuses"). We need to preserve the original historic record somewhere in a document with our reasoning why we did the switch and preserve the option to go the route C." It is an edit to the original tree and is flagged as one.
113	
114	**The decisions.** Route A (`POSITIONS.md:92`). The form, S1 (`:109`): "1, teams' way", the layered form of `explorations/reviews/spec-change-form.md` section 9, option 1. The team's later Types chapter cited beside `Specification/` wherever it covers a topic (`:110`). The per-example verdicts, S2 (`:111-130`), from `explorations/reviews/spec-refused-examples-judgement.md` sections 3 to 5 and 7. 117	- The rule, once, in Luchangco's two-part form (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:353-376`), over every static argument except operator arguments. In `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex`, beside the exclusion properties (`:210-216`), which instantiations exclude each other: two instantiations of one generic trait exclude each other unless every static argument other than an operator argument is the same; named "instantiation exclusion", the later chapter's short form, with "multiple instantiation exclusion" and the type group's paper cited (`Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`). # What the code that relies on wrapping should become

## 0. The question, and what this note read

Under `walk` (the interpreter), arithmetic on the fixed-width integers `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` *wraps*: when the true answer does not fit in 32 or 64 bits, the machine keeps its low 32 or 64 bits and throws the rest away, so `ZZ32` maximum plus one comes out as the `ZZ32` minimum. The specification says such an *overflow* (an answer outside the type's range) throws `IntegerOverflow` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, `:195-196`). Pavol decided that `walk` follows the specification (ledger row 379; `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:88`). This note asks what each of those pieces should become.

## 4. Why the count is not zero: code that relies on wrapping

The count finds two kinds of code that rely on wrapping: the library, which is the brief's second stop ("a library body that relies on wrapping"), and tests.

**Library bodies, measured.**
- **`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1030-1031`**, `CompactFullParScalarRange.generate` (object at `:1013`). It splits a range at a power-of-two boundary: `split = partitionL((lo BITXOR hi)+1)`, then `mid = hi BITAND (BITNOT (split-1))`. When the bounds straddle zero, `lo BITXOR hi` is negative, `partitionL` (the native `Integer.highestOneBit(u - 1)`, `Int.java:212-216`) returns the minimum, and `split-1` wraps to the maximum. That gives `mid = 0`, the right split, by wrapping. Every parallel `ZZ32` range with a negative lower bound and a nonnegative upper bound goes through it: `-4:4` in `setSum.fss:19` and `(-2)#10` in `simpleSum.fss:53`.
- **`RangeInternals.fss:1200-1201`**, the same shape in `StridedFullParScalarRange.generate` (object at `:1183`), met by `IntMapTest`.
- **`Library/Random.fss:234-235`**, `LinearCongruential.random`: `(mult widen(state) + add) MOD modulus`, with `mult = 25214903917` and `modulus = 2^48` (`:252-253`). The product exceeds 2^63 for nearly every state below 2^48. The answer is right today only because a wrap modulo 2^64 keeps residues modulo 2^48. `QuickCheck.fss:1151-1153` and `ReflectiveQuickCheck.fss:337-339` build every test context on it, so `QuickCheckTest`, `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest` and `RandomTest` stop before their first property.
- **`Library/ChunkedSparseArray.fss:76`**, `secondaryIndex`: `popCount((mask-1) BITAND fe)`. Here `mask = widen(1) LSHIFT (i BITAND 63)` (`:75`), which is the `ZZ64` minimum at bit 63, so `mask-1` wraps. `zeno.fss` meets it through `chunkedSparseArray`.
- **`Library/IntMap.fss:673-677`**, `keySplit`: `(-p) BITAND mx`, where `p` is a `ZZ64` `partitionL` that is the minimum when the keys straddle zero. The logging pass measures 27 `Long$Negate` overflows in `IntMapTest` after its first `Int$Sub`.

**Library bodies, by reading only.** Three more sites in `RangeInternals.fss` have the same `split-1`: `:1045-1046`, `:1220-1221` and `:1241-1242`. Each of the five `(lo BITXOR hi)+1` also overflows when `lo BITXOR hi` is the maximum, for example a range `0:2147483647`. `Random.fss:241`, `LinearCongruential.perturbed`, has the same product as `:235`. `Library/Generator22D.fss:227-238` has the same split shape four times. Its bounds are array indices, which are nonnegative, so by reading it does not overflow. The count covers only what `ProjectFortress/tests/` exercises. The library code no test reaches, and programs outside the corpus, were not measured.

**Tests that rely on wrapping.** These are the team's own tests in the 2012 tree:
- `ProjectFortress/tests/intPrim.fss:21-22` and `longPrim.fss:21-22` assert `a.minimum - 1 = a.maximum` and `a.maximum + 1 = a.minimum`, which is exactly what the specification refuses.
- `HeapTest.fss:95-99` is a multiplicative hash in `ZZ32`.
- `QuickCheckTest.fss:89-90` checks "associativity of `+` operator over `ZZ32` domain: should pass" on random `ZZ32` values, which holds only under wrapping. The logging pass meets 8 `Int$Add` overflows there.
- `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest.fss:16-17` has the same property; the logging pass meets 12 `Int$Add` overflows there.

The last two are hidden today behind the random generator's overflow, which comes first.

**The library authors knew about overflow.** `RangeInternals.fss:59` says "tries to avoid overflow", and `Random.fss:350-351` gives MT19937's seed vector the type `ZZ64` "due to the overflow mechanism". So the authors wrote parts of these files expecting overflow to be an error, and the sites above are the places where they did not.

7	Under `walk` (the interpreter), arithmetic on the fixed-width integers `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` *wraps*: when the true answer does not fit in 32 or 64 bits, the machine keeps its low 32 or 64 bits and throws the rest away, so `ZZ32` maximum plus one comes out as the `ZZ32` minimum. This note asks what each of those pieces should become.

11	## 1. Every way the language and the library offer
12	
13	Three words first. *Wrapping* arithmetic keeps the low bits of the true answer, as described above. *Checked* arithmetic gives the true answer or throws `IntegerOverflow`. *Saturating* arithmetic clamps: an answer above the maximum becomes the maximum, one below the minimum becomes the minimum.
14	
15	Code meets overflow with one of two needs. Some code *means to wrap*: it wants the answer modulo 2^32 or 2^64, as a hash function or a random-number generator does. Other code *must avoid overflow*: the answer it wants fits in the type, but a step on the way does not, or the code wants to know when an answer would not fit. Each way below says which need it serves and where it stands on each path.
16	
17	### The library's own ways
18	
19	1. **Compute where nothing can overflow, then reduce on purpose** (means to wrap). The Mersenne twister in the same file as the failing generator holds its 32-bit words in `ZZ64`, and its seeding generator multiplies there, where a 31-bit constant times a 32-bit word cannot leave 63 bits, and then keeps the low 32 bits with an explicit mask: `state := (1812433253 (state BITXOR (state RSHIFT 30)) + 1) BITAND 4294967295` (`Library/Random.fss:336`, again at `:344`; the twister itself masks its words at `:278`, `:286`). Its documentation comment names the reason, "Its seed vector is of `ZZ64` due to the overflow mechanism" (`Library/Random.fss:350-351`). This runs the same on both paths and never overflows. It needs a type twice as wide as the answer, so for 64-bit work it needs the unbounded `ZZ` (way 9).
20	2. **The named truncating conversion** (means to wrap). `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits of a `ZZ64` on both paths, decided by Pavol for row 346 (`POSITIONS.md:76`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Long.java:248-252` is `(int) x`; the compiled body `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:659`). So `narrow(widen(c1) widen(n) + widen(c2))` is an exact 32-bit wrap with no overflow anywhere. `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` (to `ZZ32` and to `ZZ64`) also keep the low bits under `walk`, `BigInteger.intValue` and `longValue` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:891-895`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/BigNum.java:286-296`); that truncation is not a decision on record, only the tree's behaviour.
21	3. **Reorder the computation so no step leaves the range** (must avoid overflow). `meetingPoint` in the range library "tries to avoid overflow" by stepping from one bound towards the other instead of multiplying strides (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:58-79`). 43	## 2. The refresher: what the three kinds of arithmetic mean
44	
45	- An integer in mathematics has no size. A 32-bit word has 2^32 bit patterns, and in *two's complement*, the layout every JVM uses, they stand for -2^31 through 2^31-1, the top bit counting as -2^31.
46	- **Wrapping** is arithmetic *modulo* 2^32 (or 2^64): two integers count as the same when they differ by a multiple of 2^32. That arithmetic is a *ring*: `+` and multiplication are associative and commutative, multiplication distributes over `+`, and every value has a negative. So every identity built only from `+`, `-` and multiplication holds exactly, for instance `(p ∔ q) ∔ r = p ∔ (q ∔ r)` for all `p`, `q`, `r`. Order does not survive: the maximum ∔ 1 is below the maximum. Wrapping is the right meaning when a program cares about the answer modulo 2^n, as hashes, random-number generators, checksums and bit masks do, and the wrong one when it cares about how big a number is.
47	- **Checked** arithmetic is a partial operation: every answer it gives is the true integer answer, so a program that finishes has computed exactly what the unbounded integers would. Laws such as associativity hold wherever both sides answer, but one side can throw where the other does not: `(MAX + 1) + (-1)` throws, `MAX + (1 + (-1))` is `MAX`.
48	- **Saturating** arithmetic never throws and never wraps, and it is not associative: `(MAX ⊞ 1) ⊞ (-1)` is `MAX - 1`, `MAX ⊞ (1 ⊞ (-1))` is `MAX`. It suits signals, pixel values and counters that should stick at their limit. In the specification the boxed operators mean "toward zero" on floats too, rounding toward zero (`opr-overview.tex:181`, `:214`), and a clamp is the representable value nearest the true answer on the side of zero, so the box family is one idea across both kinds of number.
49	- **The bit identities three of the library sites use.** For a power of two `p`, `p - 1` is the mask of the bits below `p`, and `-p` is the mask of the bits at and above it. For positive `p` both are ordinary integers that fit. When `p` is the sign bit alone, which as a number is the minimum, the true values of `p - 1` and `-p` do not fit, but their wrapped values, the maximum and the minimum, are exactly the masks wanted. Those sites are right *because* the machine wraps: they are modular arithmetic spelled with the ordinary operators.

60	## 4. What the specification says, under every spelling
61	
62	- **The rule**, stated twice: "The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced. For integer results, overflow throws an `IntegerOverflow`. Rational computations do not overflow." (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-156` for multiplication and division, `:195-197` for addition and subtraction).
63	- **The spellings**: wraparound ∔, ∸ and ⨰, saturating ⊞, ⊟, ⊡ or ⊠, "These operations do not overflow" (`:172-176`, `:205-209`). Steele's 2012 rewrite of the prose keeps both paragraphs word for word (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Operators/operator-overview.tick:154-155`, `:172-176`, `:195-196`, `:205-209`, added in `91e71e62e`, 2012-05-28, "Spec has new directory Language/Operators").
64	- **The integer chapter.** `ZZ` extends `CommutativeRing[\ZZ,∔,∸,⨰\]` beside the rings of the plain and the boxed operators (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:196-203`); the identities of ∔ and ⨰ are 0 and 1 (`:337-341`); on `ZZ` they equal the plain operators "because operations on type ℤ never need to wrap or saturate" (`:359`, `:369-370`, `:385`, `:400-401`, `:416`). The chapter is about `ZZ`; it names no fixed-width type.
65	- **The same idea under another spelling**: the binary-word methods of way 10 (`Specification/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1172-1235`, `:1510-1514`), where wrapping, carry-out, a caller-supplied overflow action, saturation and the double-width product are method names on the layer the fixed widths are to be built from.
66	- **The precedence appendix** (way 12): ∔ and ∸ mix only with each other and bind looser than ⨰ (`Specification/appendices/operators.tex:215-224`).
67	- **What 1.0 said.** The published 1.0 specification (2008-03-31, `403afbe0b`; the same file is `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`), the version cut down to what the interpreter implemented, has no overflow rule and lists `DOTPLUS` and `BOXPLUS` only in its precedence appendix (text extracted with `pdftotext`; its one mention of `IntegerOverflow` is the object's declaration).
68	- **What it does not say.** Nothing in the specification tells a hash or a random-number generator which family to use; it supplies the spellings and the default.

71	
72	- The interpreter's library nests `ZZ32` inside `ZZ64` inside `ZZ` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:465`, `:499`, `:537`) and `NN32` inside `NN64` inside `ZZ` (`:438`; `NN32` itself in `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:82`). 73	- Route A (`POSITIONS.md:92`) flattens the tower into siblings, each with its own algebra, a wider type converting from a narrower one. Each fixed width is then its own ring under ∔, ∸ and ⨰: the integers modulo 2^32 and modulo 2^64 are different rings, and a `ZZ32` ∔ `ZZ64` converts to `ZZ64` first and wraps at 64 bits.

85	
86	Each quotation below was fetched on 2026-09-26 unless marked otherwise.
87	
88	**JVM family**
89	- **Java.** `+` wraps silently: "If an integer addition overflows, then the result is the low-order bits of the mathematical sum as represented in some sufficiently large two's-complement format" (JLS § 15.18.2, <https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-15.html>; not fetched, the chapter is too long for the fetch tool, quoted from the standard's text). Checking is a library method: `Math.addExact` "Returns the sum of its arguments, throwing an exception if the result overflows an `int`", since Java 8; the high half of a product is `Math.multiplyHigh`, since Java 9 (<https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Math.html>).
90	- **X10**, IBM's language from the same DARPA programme as Fortress, compiled to Java and C++: `Int`'s `+` and `*` say "Overflows result in truncating the high bits" and are the bare expressions `((#this) + (#x))` in both back ends (<https://raw.githubusercontent.com/x10-lang/x10/master/x10.runtime/src-x10/x10/lang/Int.x10>). There is no checked operator.
91	
92	**Close to the metal**
93	- **Swift.** "By default Swift reports an error rather than allowing an invalid value to be created. However, when you specifically want an overflow condition to truncate the number of available bits, you can opt in to this behavior … Overflow addition (`&+`), Overflow subtraction (`&-`), Overflow multiplication (`&*`)" (The Swift Programming Language, Advanced Operators, <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift-book/main/TSPL.docc/LanguageGuide/AdvancedOperators.md>). The error stops the program; it cannot be caught.
94	- **Rust.** "If a program contains arithmetic overflow, the programmer has made an error. In the following discussion, we maintain a distinction between arithmetic overflow and wrapping arithmetic. The first is erroneous, while the second is intentional." Builds with debug assertions must panic; "Other kinds of builds may result in panics or silently wrapped values on overflow, at the implementation's discretion"; "`i32::wrapping_add` provides two's complement, wrapping addition", and "a `Wrapping<T>` newtype … ensures all standard arithmetic operations for `T` have wrapping semantics" (Rust Reference, <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/behavior-not-considered-unsafe.html>). The standard library adds `checked_add`, "returning `None` if overflow occurred", `saturating_add` and `overflowing_add` (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.i32.html>).
95	- **Zig.** "Operators such as `+` and `-` cause Illegal Behavior on integer overflow"; `+%` wraps, `+|` saturates, and `@addWithOverflow` reports the overflow beside the result (<https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/>).
96	- **C.** Signed overflow is undefined behaviour and unsigned arithmetic is reduced modulo 2^n (C11 § 6.5 ¶ 5, § 6.2.5 ¶ 9; not fetched).
97	
98	**Scientific**
99	- **Julia.** "In Julia, exceeding the maximum representable value of a given type results in a wraparound behavior"; "The `Base.Checked` module provides a suite of arithmetic operations equipped with overflow checks"; where overflow cannot be tolerated, `BigInt` (manual, Integers and Floating-Point Numbers, <https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/integers-and-floating-point-numbers/>). 103	- **Python.** "Integers have unlimited precision." (<https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html>). Fortress's `ZZ` is in this family.

105	**Reading.** The specification's design is Swift's (an error by default, wrapping only under its own operator), with the saturating family as operators, as Zig has them, and a catchable exception where Swift stops the program; the Fortress text predates Swift's 2014 release (section 8). Of the four peers Pavol named, Swift and Rust separate "meant to wrap" from "overflowed by mistake" in the spelling; Julia and X10 wrap everything, Julia for loop speed. 137	## 9. The derivation from Pavol's principle, case by case
138	
139	The principle (`POSITIONS.md:72`, 2026-09-22): use the JVM's defaults where they make sense; correct the JVM's mistakes through the lens of a high-performance, mathematically precise language; where hardware behaviour is expressible in bytecode it gets its own explicit spelling, in the family the specification already has for wrapping and saturating.
140	
141	**In general.** The JVM's default `+` wraps (JLS § 15.18.2). The specification, and Pavol's decision on row 379, correct that: `+` is checked. The hardware behaviour, the wrap, is a single `iadd`, `isub`, `imul`, `ladd`, `lsub` or `lmul`, and the specification's spelling for it is ∔, ∸, ⨰. So code that means to wrap should say ∔, ∸ or ⨰. Code that must avoid overflow should be reordered so that the checked operators never trip, as the library already does (way 3), and not respelled with a wrap it does not mean.
142	
143	**Costs on the JVM**, by reading; none of these was measured for this note.
144	- ∔, ∸, ⨰: the plain instruction, with no branch. They are what the compiled prelude's Wrapping natives already are (`simpleIntArith.java:224-234`).
145	- Checked `+`: a sign test and a branch that is never taken (`simpleIntArith.java:62-66`), or `Math.addExact`, which the JIT compiles to the processor's overflow flag. The performance roadmap notes that the branch may keep a loop from being vectorised (`explorations/performance-roadmap.md:90-100`, read from HotSpot's documented rules, unmeasured).
146	- A reordering: one comparison, or the same subtractions in another order; nothing measurable.
147	- `ZZ`: a `BigInteger` object for every operation, allocated and collected.
148	- A clamp: a comparison and a branch per operation.
149	- The interpreter's own speed does not enter any decision (`POSITIONS.md:38`).
150	
151	**Case by case.** Each case says what the code means, what it becomes under the principle, and the alternative from section 1 with its cost.
152	
153	- **(a) The range split's `split-1`**, six sites: `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1031`, `:1046`, `:1201`, `:1221`, `:1242`, `:1266`. Row 403 and rung O's report list five; `:1266`, the loop's negative-stride branch, has the same text (by reading). It means a bit mask (section 2). It becomes `hi BITAND (BITNOT (split DOTMINUS 1))`: the same value as today, and no cost. Alternative: say "split at zero" in words, `if lo < 0 AND 0 <= hi then 0 else hi BITAND (BITNOT (split - 1)) end` (written with the element type's own zero in the generic code), which costs a comparison per split and changes Maessen's text more. A third, the compiled library's midpoint split through `floorAverage` (section 6), never overflows but moves every split point off the power-of-two boundaries Maessen chose, so it is a redesign, not a repair.
154	- **(b) The range split's `(lo BITXOR hi)+1`**, the same six sites. It overflows only when `lo BITXOR hi` is the maximum, for instance on a range `0:2147483647` (by reading), and `partitionL` then subtracts the 1 again inside Java, so the pair computes the highest set bit of `lo BITXOR hi`. It becomes `(lo BITXOR hi) DOTPLUS 1`, exact at no cost. Alternative: a primitive that gives the highest set bit directly, the specification's `leftmostOneBit` (`binary.tex:1289`, `:1464`), which removes the `+1`; that is a new native no site needs.
155	- **(c) The strided distance `(…) - lo - 1`**, four sites: `:1201`, `:1221`, `:1242`, `:1266`. It means an ordinary distance, and that distance fits whenever `mid > lo`, which always holds, but its first step `mid - lo` overflows when `lo` is the minimum and `mid` is 0 (by reading, row 403). This is must-avoid, not means-to-wrap: reorder it as `(mid - 1) - lo`, with `mid` named first, and keep the checked operators.
156	- **(d) `LinearCongruential`**, `Library/Random.fss:235` (measured) and `:241` (by reading). It means arithmetic modulo 2^48, done through arithmetic modulo 2^64. It becomes `((mult DOTTIMES widen(state)) DOTPLUS add) MOD modulus`: the same values, no cost, `MOD` bringing a negative wrapped value back into range as it does today. This is right only because 2^48 divides 2^64. The object is generic in its modulus (`Random.fss:222`) and built once, with 2^48 (`:253`); for a modulus that is not a power of two, today's code and this one both give wrong numbers without a word (section 11). Alternatives: exact through `ZZ`, right for every modulus, at a `BigInteger` per random number (`QuickCheckTest` alone meets 146K overflowing products); or the Mersenne twister's habit (way 1), splitting the state into 24-bit halves so every product fits, about five lines and three multiplications.
157	- **(e) `ChunkedSparseArray.secondaryIndex`**, `Library/ChunkedSparseArray.fss:76` (measured). It means the bits below the mask. It becomes `popCount((mask DOTMINUS 1) BITAND fe)`. Alternatives: `if mask < 0 then BITNOT mask else mask - 1 end`, or, from the bit index `indexAndMask` already computes (`:75`), `BITNOT (widen(-1) LSHIFT b)` (way 4).
158	- **(f) `IntMap.keySplit`**, `Library/IntMap.fss:675-676`: the negation at `:676` measured (27 `Long$Negate`), `mn-1` at `:675` by reading when the smaller key is the minimum. Both are bit masks. They become `p = partitionL(((mn DOTMINUS 1) BITXOR mx) DOTPLUS 1)` and `(DOTMINUS p) BITAND mx`. Alternative: a sign case, since the negated `p` is the minimum exactly when the keys straddle zero, where the answer is 0.
159	- **(g) `HeapTest`'s `spread`**, `ProjectFortress/tests/HeapTest.fss:95-99`. It means a scramble modulo 2^32: with `c1` odd, `n ↦ c1 n + c2` maps `ZZ32` onto itself one to one, so the test's keys stay distinct. It becomes `((c1 DOTTIMES n) DOTPLUS c2, n)`. Alternative: `narrow(widen(c1) widen(n) + widen(c2))` (way 2), which never overflows and gives the same value.
160	- **(h) `intPrim.fss:21-22` and `longPrim.fss:21-22`.** They assert of `+` and `-` exactly what the specification refuses; their author's intent (section 8) was "the boundary behaves as it should". Under the specification the wrap identity belongs to the wrapping operators and the plain ones throw, so each file asserts both: `a.minimum DOTMINUS 1 = a.maximum` and `a.maximum DOTPLUS 1 = a.minimum`, and, with a copy of rung I's helper, `overflows(fn () => a.minimum - 1)` and `overflows(fn () => a.maximum + 1)`. `longPrim`'s `a: ZZ64 = 0` holds a `ZZ32` (row 146), so all four test 32 bits there until `a` is set with `widen(0)`; that is row 146's correction, not this one's.
161	- **(i) The associativity properties**, `QuickCheckTest.fss:89-90` and `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest.fss:16-17`: "associativity of `+` operator over `ZZ32` domain: should pass", set against `RR64`'s "may fail". Under checked `+` associativity is not a total property of `ZZ32` (section 2). The ring the specification declares for it is ∔, so the property becomes `(p DOTPLUS q) DOTPLUS r = p DOTPLUS (q DOTPLUS r)` and still should pass. Alternatives: keep `+` and state the property only where it answers, "`+` agrees with ℤ wherever it answers", with `==>` over the sums computed in `ZZ` or with the generator held to its levels 0-2 (way 11); or move the property to `ZZ`.
162	
163	**One thing all cases share.** A `ZZ64` variable that holds a `ZZ32` value (row 146) wraps at 32 bits under ∔ exactly as it does under `+` today; the respelling keeps today's values, that quirk included. Fixing row 146 is its own row.
164	
165	## 10. The options as they would be put to Pavol
166	
167	**Option 1, the specification's own way.** Declare ∔, ∸ (unary and binary) and ⨰ in the interpreter's library, on `Integral[\I\]` and on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`; rewrite the sites of section 9 with them; reorder the strided distance; then land rung O.
168	- *What the work does.* Under `walk` the new operators are bound to wrapping natives: on `NN32` and `NN64` to the natives `+` uses today, unchanged; on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` to new small wrapping classes, because rung O's patch turns today's classes into checked ones (four a width: add, subtract, multiply, negate); on `ZZ` to the exact ones, as the specification says.
169	- *What it produces.* Every site gives the value it gives today, because the wrapping operator is the arithmetic the site gets today. So rung O's count is expected to fall to zero. That has to be measured with the same runner, not assumed.
170	- *What it touches.* `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi` and `.fss` (for `NN32`), about 50 lines; `Int.java` and `Long.java`, eight small classes; `RangeInternals.fss` (about 16 lines at the six sites), `Random.fss` (2), `ChunkedSparseArray.fss` (1), `IntMap.fss` (2); five tests (about 12 lines). All are edits to the original tree and are flagged as such. It adds one gated test of ∔, ∸ and ⨰ at both widths' boundaries, and the rung declares its checker count, since `Integral` gains declarations.
171	- *What it commits him to.* Row 348 is decided for the specification's spelling in the one library. The compiled prelude's reversed operators leave with the prelude at the switch-over, and the compiled tests that use them are respelled then: 10 files, 138 matching lines (`Integer3`, `Integer4`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `AverageTest` and `ShiftTest2` in `library_tests/`; `IntegerLiteralsFolding`, `IntSemanticsRungB` and `XXXBoxDotSpellingsRungW` in `compiler_tests/`), with `BOXCROSS` becoming ⨰. The saturating family stays undeclared in the one library until a step of its own. It shares `FortressLibrary.fsi`/`.fss` with the tower-flattening rung, so the manifest orders the two.
172	- *Variant 1b.* The three bit-mask cases (a), (e) and (f) written with explicit sign cases instead of ∸, and the wrapping operators kept for the generator, the hash and the tests. The commitments are the same; there is more text to review, and "split at zero" is said in words.
173	
174	**Option 2, restructure everything and declare no operator.** Every site is rewritten in the library's avoid-overflow habits: the zero case in the split, a highest-set-bit primitive or a guard for the `+1`, masks by shift, a sign case in `IntMap`, the hash through `widen` and `narrow`, the generator exact through `ZZ` or by split multiplication, and the tests asserting the throw, with the properties restated on the range where `+` answers.
175	- *What it commits him to.* No new operator, and row 348 stays open. After the switch-over the one library has no spelling for a wrap at all, so the team's compiled tests that wrap with `BOXCROSS` and `BOXPLUS` lose their operator. Each site's reasoning changes, not just its spelling. The generator costs either a `BigInteger` per random number or a five-line split multiplication. The two QuickCheck tests test different properties from today's. Under his principle, the hardware behaviour is left without its explicit spelling.
176	
177	**Option 3, the whole family now.** Option 1, plus the saturating operators ⊞, ⊟, ⊡ and ⊠ in the same rung (new clamping natives under `walk`, about eight small classes).
178	- *What it commits him to.* The same as option 1, plus declarations that no site uses yet, and a gated test for both families. The protocol's "one variable per step" argues for doing it later.
179	
180	**Not an option.** Keeping `walk` wrapping would reverse row 379, and the compiled path throws on these same bodies at the switch-over anyway (row 403).
181	
182	**Recommendation (my reading, not a decision):** option 1: declare ∔, ∸ and ⨰ in the one library, respell the wrap-reliant sites and tests with them, and reorder the strided distance, as the step before rung O; the saturating family gets a later step of its own.
183	
184	## 11. Found on the way
185	
186	- **A sixth split site.** `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1265-1266` has the same `split-1` and the same distance as the five that row 403 and rung O's report list (by reading).
187	- **The unsigned types wrap under `walk` and row 379 does not cover them.** `NN32` and `NN64` arithmetic goes through `com.naturalbridge.misc.Unsigned.add`, `subtract` and `multiplyTo…`, which are bare `iadd` and `lmul` (read with `javap`; `NN32.java:103-124`, `UnsignedLong.java:104-125`), while the compiled path's `NN32` `+` throws (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:768`). Steele's gated `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss:195-211` (`dc41d5000`, 2008-07-21) uses unary `-` on an unsigned value as 2^w minus that value. It is the same question as this note's, larger, and it comes later, when the unsigned natives are checked.
188	- **`LinearCongruential` is wrong for most moduli.** The object is generic in its modulus, but wrapping modulo 2^64 and then taking `MOD modulus` is right only when the modulus is a power of two; the library builds it only with 2^48 (`Library/Random.fss:222`, `:253`).
189	- **A wrapping operator under `walk` needs natives of its own.** Rung O's patch changes today's ten natives in place (`REPORT.md` § 3), so after it no native wraps; a wrapping operator bound to the old names would start to throw.
190	- **The box family means "toward zero" on both kinds of number.** Saturation clamps toward zero, and the same boxed operators on floats round toward zero (`opr-overview.tex:181`, `:214`). That is a design reason behind the specification's pairing, relevant to row 348.

4. Add one gated test that checks the three operators wrap at the minimum and maximum of both widths, citing `opr-overview.tex:172-176` and `:205-209`.
